message.content:
Research + design task (research only; do not modify files). Context: we're building a web app on the Claude API that turns any topic a user wants to learn into a "video game" for one learning session. Structure: Game → Sections → Units (small dose of exposition, then application questions) with a mid-section mini-boss (cumulative check) and an end-of-section boss (cumulative Q&A/application, may reference prior sections), plus a final boss covering the whole game. Nothing is pre-scripted: questions, section length, even story length must adapt to user performance, targeting ~80%+ correct. After the game, an epilogue proposes a sequel game (next session); users can have multiple topic series, resume mid-game, and request "side stories" to review a past concept. Must be buildable as a prototype in ~2 days by one engineer with Claude Code.

Research and recommend:
1. Curriculum generation: how to have an LLM generate a concept map / skill graph / learning objectives for an arbitrary topic, sized to the user's stated time and scope. Evidence/approaches from LLM tutoring work (e.g., Khanmigo, Duolingo Max, Google LearnLM, Anthropic's Claude for Education "learning mode", research papers on LLM-generated quizzes/question quality).
2. Lazy vs. up-front generation: generate a skeleton outline up front (sections + concepts), then generate each unit's content/questions just-in-time based on performance. Trade-offs on latency, coherence, cost.
3. Adaptivity: lightweight learner model suitable for a prototype — per-concept mastery estimate (simple Elo, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, or rolling accuracy), rules for: when to add an extra unit, when to skip ahead, when to trigger mini-boss/boss, how to pick difficulty to hold ~80-85% success, and how to choose concepts for cumulative boss questions (spaced/interleaved retrieval).
4. Question formats and grading: multiple choice vs. free-response graded by Claude; pros/cons for application-focused learning; using structured outputs (JSON schema) for question objects; ensuring correctness of generated answers (self-check, second pass); feedback that explains errors.
5. Data model: a simple schema for User, Series(topic), Game, Section, Unit, Question, Attempt, ConceptMastery, StoryState — and what state needs to be passed to Claude on each call.
6. Biggest risks (hallucinated facts, too-easy questions, latency between questions, cost) and mitigations.

Return a concise but concrete report (≤ 900 words) with a recommended architecture, a sketch of the per-turn loop, and sources with URLs. Flag uncertainty; don't fabricate.

The paper is "The Eighty Five Percent Rule for Optimal Learning" by Robert C. Wilson, Amitai Shenhav, Mark Straccia, and Jonathan D. Cohen, published in Nature Communications (2019, DOI 10.1038/s41467-019-12552-4).

- **Core finding:** The authors describe a "sweet spot" where training is neither too easy nor too hard. For stochastic gradient-descent learning algorithms in binary classification, the optimal training error rate is about 15.87%, or roughly 85% accuracy. In many situations we find that there is a sweet spot in which training is neither too easy nor too hard, and where learning progresses most quickly. For all of these stochastic gradient-descent based learning algorithms, we find that the optimal error rate for training is around 15.87% or, conversely, that the optimal training accuracy is about 85%.
- **Evidence:** The rule came from machine-learning experiments on simple two-choice tasks. Its authors also say it holds in previous studies of animal learning, and the paper reports it works for artificial neural networks and for biologically plausible neural networks.
- **Caveats:** Wilson's own framing is limited to two-choice tasks. The search turned up several recent arXiv and related papers on using LLMs to build prerequisite and concept graphs for education.

- **Prerequisite extraction is the hard part.** One 2026 paper notes that automated prerequisite edge extraction is substantially harder and typically requires significant human correction than concept discovery. It frames LLM-based knowledge graph construction as a move to generative extraction of entity-relation triples from raw text (LLM-based knowledge graph construction (KGC) shifts this from statistical classification to generative extraction).
- **Question-bank graphs.** Auto-HKG (arXiv 2602.00020) is an LLM pipeline that builds a graph from question banks. ## Recommended architecture: a light upfront outline, content generated per unit, and a deterministic learner model

**Core principle:** let code (a small state machine) decide when to advance, remediate or trigger a boss and how hard the next question should be. Let Claude write the questions, explanations and story, grade answers, and check its own content. This keeps adaptivity testable and keeps prompts short. Khan Academy found that long prompts make the model "randomly ignore" instructions, and that putting good context in front of the model before it reasons improved accuracy.

### 1. Curriculum generation
- One call to a strong model with a JSON schema returns a **skill graph**: 6–15 concepts, sized to stated time at roughly 5–8 minutes per concept. Each concept has an id, name, learning objective (a Bloom verb such as apply/analyze), prerequisite ids, common misconceptions and "anchor facts". Concepts are grouped into 3–5 sections in prerequisite order, along with the story premise and a final-boss scenario.
- Evidence: research reports LLMs are workable at finding concepts but **prerequisite edges are less reliable** (arXiv 2504.08856; InstructKG 2602.17111; ACE, JEDM). Mitigation: validate the graph as a DAG in code, and let the user edit or confirm scope in a 10-second "quest map" screen.
- LearnLM frames pedagogy as instruction-following through system prompts. That fits a system-prompt-driven design. Claude for Education's Learning mode uses Socratic prompting. Neither publishes a curriculum-generation recipe, so this design is my synthesis, not something either documents.

### 2. Upfront vs. on-demand generation
- **Upfront:** only the outline and story arc (one call, about 5–15 seconds behind a loading animation). This keeps the story and section boundaries consistent.
- **On demand (JIT):** each unit (exposition plus a batch of 3–4 questions at the targeted difficulty) is generated when the learner reaches it. **Prefetch the next unit while the user answers the current one**, which hides most of the latency. Regenerate only if mastery moves enough to change the plan.
- Trade-off: on-demand costs more calls but keeps content adaptive and avoids wasting tokens on content the learner never reaches. Put the stable prefix (system prompt, skill graph, story bible) first and use **prompt caching** to cut cost and latency.

### 3. Learner model (prototype-sized)
- For each concept, store an **Elo-style score** θ_c, and give each question a difficulty b from 1 to 5 mapped to an Elo scale. Predicted p = σ(θ_c − b), updated by θ_c += K·(correct − p) with K about 0.4 (decay it over time). This is simpler than BKT and gives difficulty targeting for free. Duolingo's Birdbrain likewise jointly estimates learner ability and item difficulty, but I couldn't confirm that it uses Elo specifically.
- **Difficulty selection:** pick b so that p ≈ 0.82. The "85% rule" (Wilson et al., 2019) is derived for gradient-descent learners on binary tasks, so treat it as a heuristic, not proven for human concept learning.
- **Rules:**
  - Mastered = p at difficulty 3 ≥ 0.8 and at least 3 attempts.
  - Two misses in a row, or rolling accuracy below 60% over 4 attempts → insert a remediation unit targeting the misconception that was hit.
  - The first 2 answers correct at difficulty ≥ 4 → offer "skip ahead" to the mini-boss.
  - **Mini-boss** once half the section's concepts are mastered. **Boss** when all are, with a cap on units per section.
- **Choosing boss questions:** weight each concept by (1 − mastery) + time since last seen, with about 30% drawn from prior sections (interleaved and spaced retrieval; testing-effect literature such as Roediger & Karpicke 2006). Prefer multi-concept application scenarios. The final boss samples across the whole graph the same way.

### 4. Question formats and grading
- **Mix:** MCQ (instant, deterministic grading; distractors map to misconceptions, which makes errors diagnostic) for early units. Short free-response application questions graded by Claude for bosses.
- Grading evidence varies widely: from kappa about 0 (postgraduate medicine, arXiv 2505.04645) to about 0.9 with clear rubrics (arXiv 2511.10819). **So grade free responses against a rubric generated with the question** (key points, plus accept/partial/reject examples). Return correct/partial/incorrect, the misconception, and feedback. Don't penalize Elo harshly for "partial".
- **Structured outputs** (`output_config.format` json_schema or strict tool use) guarantee the shape but not the correctness.
- **Correctness:** use a cheap second pass where a verifier model answers the question blind. Discard the question if its answer doesn't match the key or if it judges the question ambiguous. Khan Academy offloads arithmetic to a calculator; do the same with a code tool for math topics.
- Feedback explains why the chosen distractor is wrong and links back to the exposition.

### 5. Data model
- User
- Series(id, user, topic, scope)
- Game(id, series, skill_graph JSON, story_bible JSON, status, current_section/unit)
- Section(id, game, idx, concept_ids, state: units|miniboss|boss|done)
- Unit(id, section, kind: lesson|remediation|side_story|miniboss|boss, concept_ids, exposition, story_beat)
- Question(id, unit, concept_ids, format, difficulty, stem, options, answer_key, rubric, misconception_map, verified)
- Attempt(id, question, response, grade, misconception, latency_ms, ts)
- ConceptMastery(user, series, concept_id, theta, n_attempts, last_seen)
- StoryState(game, summary ≤200 words, characters, open_threads)

Resuming a game means reloading the Game pointers. A side story is a Unit with kind=side_story pointing at past concepts. The sequel game is seeded from the epilogue output plus the Series' mastery table.

**Per-call context sent to Claude:** cached prefix (system rules, skill graph, story bible). Then the variable part: target concepts, objective, misconceptions, target difficulty, compact mastery summary, last 3–5 attempt results, StoryState summary, and the output schema. Never send the full transcript.

### Per-turn loop
1. User answers → grade (MCQ in code; free response through a Claude grader call).
2. Update Elo, log the Attempt, stream feedback.
3. State machine picks the next step (next question, remediation, skip, mini-boss/boss, section end).
4. If the next question batch was already generated and verified, serve it. Otherwise generate, verify and serve.
5. Kick off prefetch of the next unit in the background.
6. At section end: the Claude call that writes the boss scenario also updates StoryState (`story_update` field).

### 6. Risks and mitigations
- **Hallucinated facts:** verifier pass, anchor facts in the outline, a "report question" button, and a mostly-MCQ mix for factual topics.
- **Too-easy questions:** require apply/analyze objectives and scenario stems. If accuracy stays above 90%, raise b. Check a sample of distractors in evals. Literature warns of "superficial distractors" (Grevisse et al., 2024).
- **Latency:** prefetch, streaming, a fast model (Haiku-class) for grading and verifying, and a strong model for the outline and bosses.
- **Cost:** prompt caching, batched question generation (3–4 per call), and a compact state summary.
- **Story bloat:** cap story beats at 2–3 sentences per unit and scale them down when performance drops.
- **Open question:** whether ~80% targeting works for conceptual (non-perceptual) learning is untested here. Log the data so it can be tuned.

### Sources
- Claude for Education / Learning mode: https://www.anthropic.com/news/introducing-claude-for-education
- LearnLM report: https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16429v2 ; https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/learnlm-technical-report/
- Khanmigo math and prompting: https://blog.khanacademy.org/khanmigo-math-computation-and-tutoring-updates/ ; https://blog.khanacademy.org/khan-academys-7-step-approach-to-prompt-engineering-for-khanmigo
- Duolingo Birdbrain: https://blog.duolingo.com/learning-how-to-help-you-learn-introducing-birdbrain ; https://spectrum.ieee.org/duolingo
- 85% rule: https://experts.arizona.edu/en/publications/the-eighty-five-percent-rule-for-optimal-learning/ (Nature Comms, DOI 10.1038/s41467-019-12552-4)
- LLM concept and prerequisite graphs: https://arxiv.org/html/2504.08856v1 ; https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2602.17111v1 ; https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/737
- LLM MCQ quality: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42979-024-02963-6 ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.13439v2.pdf
- LLM grading agreement: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04645v1 ; https://arxiv.org/html/2511.10819v2
- Claude structured outputs: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs ; prompt caching: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
- BKT (Corbett & Anderson 1994) and Roediger & Karpicke 2006 are cited from memory as standard references; I did not fetch them. Duolingo Max internals are not covered because I found no technical source.
